metadata.title: May 2025 surveillance of cataracts in adults: management (NICE guideline NG77)
metadata.summary: This surveillance report assesses whether new evidence warrants changes to NICE's guideline on managing cataracts in adults. It reviews biometry formulas, intraocular lens selection, surgical timing and technique, bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery, and toric lenses. It proposes updating guidance on intraocular lens material and design, while retaining the existing guidance in the other areas.

toxicities.incidence: Donachie et al. 2023 observed PCO in 12.3% of eyes in an analysis of 500,872 cataract surgeries. The RCOphth 2021 audit reported PCO rates of 4% at 1 year, 18.0% at 3 years and 31% at 5 years. The report also describes PCO as occurring in roughly 1 in 5 eyes after cataract surgery.
prevention: Evidence reviewed in the report associates hydrophobic lenses, and potentially silicone lenses, with less PCO than hydrophilic lenses; the report proposes updating guidance on IOL material rather than issuing a new recommendation here.
Evidence suggests that sharp-edged IOLs are likely associated with less PCO than round-edged IOLs; the report proposes updating guidance on lens design.

toxicities.incidence: Dickman et al. 2022 found a very low risk of unilateral endophthalmitis in both groups and no reports of bilateral endophthalmitis. None of the included studies was powered to detect bilateral endophthalmitis.

conditions.name: cataracts in adults
conditions.description: Cataracts are generally associated with ageing. The document examines cataract surgery, including intraocular lens selection, lens-power calculation, surgical technique and the timing of surgery in both eyes.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported cataract prevalence rises with age: 24% at 70 to 74 years, 42% at 75 to 79 years, 59% at 80 to 84 years, and 71% among people over 85 years. Around 472,000 cataract operations take place each year in the NHS in England and Wales.

subtypes.name: eyes with short axial lengths
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Axial length less than 22.00 mm; the guideline evidence considered lens-power formulas separately for this group.

subtypes.name: eyes with very long axial lengths
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Axial length greater than 26.00 mm; the guideline evidence considered lens-power formulas separately for this group.

subtypes.name: eyes with a history of corneal refractive surgery
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Previous corneal refractive surgery affects lens-power calculation; the guideline evidence did not identify a formula with consistently better results for this group.

subtypes.name: patients with astigmatism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Preoperative astigmatism is considered when comparing toric lenses with other approaches to cataract surgery.

subtypes.name: people at low risk of intra- or postoperative complications
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The evidence assessed for bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery came from carefully selected people at low risk of surgical complications.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure ocular parameters for intraocular lens power calculation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before cataract surgery when calculating intraocular lens power.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline evidence assessed formula accuracy by axial length and prior corneal refractive surgery; the surveillance review did not find sufficient evidence to change the formula recommendations.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure the cornea when assessing a toric lens.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The committee identified this as potential additional preoperative biometry for toric lenses and noted that it was not available in all centres.

long_term_effects: Posterior capsule opacification (PCO) can occur after cataract surgery.

conditions.name: posterior capsule opacification (PCO)
conditions.description: A complication following cataract surgery whose occurrence varies with intraocular lens characteristics. The surveillance report proposes updating the guideline's lens material and design recommendations to address PCO.
conditions.epidemiology: The document describes PCO as occurring in roughly 1 in 5 eyes after cataract surgery. Donachie et al. 2023 observed PCO in 12.3% of eyes in an analysis of 500,872 cataract operations, with rates increasing over time. In the RCOphth 2021 audit, observed rates were 4% at 1 year, 18.0% at 3 years and 31% at 5 years; the report cautioned that variation in how PCO was recorded over time made comparisons between specific lens models difficult.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The RCOphth 2021 audit authors advised centres to improve PCO recording and compare rates across intraocular lenses. The audit could not link a patient's cataract operation and subsequent PCO YAG when these occurred at different centres.

conditions.name: astigmatism
conditions.description: Preoperative astigmatism is considered in decisions about cataract surgery, including comparisons of toric lenses with non-toric lenses or incision-based approaches. The guideline retains a research recommendation concerning the cost-effectiveness of these approaches.

subtypes.name: significant preoperative astigmatism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The 2021 surveillance review described mixed evidence on whether FLACS improves astigmatism outcomes in this cataract-surgery subgroup.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure corneal characteristics when assessing a toric lens.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The committee identified it as potential additional preoperative biometry associated with toric lenses.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The committee discussed the possible need for additional appointments after toric lens implantation to check refractive correction; it did not specify a follow-up schedule.

recommendations.statement: Use laser-assisted cataract surgery only in the context of clinical trials.
recommendations.context: Recommendation 1.6.1 addresses surgical timing and technique.
recommendations.rationale: The committee found no clinically meaningful advantage over standard phacoemulsification and considered routine use inappropriate.

recommendations.statement: Offer bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery as an option only to people at low risk of complications during or after surgery, or to those requiring general anaesthesia when anaesthesia may carry risks.
recommendations.context: The review retained the existing recommendations 1.6.2 to 1.6.4; a proposed change to recommendation 1.6.3 was not adopted.
recommendations.rationale: The studies involved carefully selected, lower-risk patients and were too small to establish whether rare, catastrophic complications differ between surgical approaches.

recommendations.statement: Investigate the cost-effectiveness of toric lenses against on-axis or limbal-relaxing incision surgery, and against non-toric lenses without further intervention, in the NHS. Account for costs across the preoperative and postoperative care pathway and stratify findings by preoperative astigmatism level.
recommendations.rationale: Although toric lenses improved some visual and refractive outcomes compared with non-toric lenses, their effect on quality of life and their cost-effectiveness remained uncertain.

recommendations.context: The document refers to an existing 'do not do' recommendation for multifocal lenses in section 8.3 of the full guideline; it does not reproduce that recommendation's wording.
recommendations.rationale: The committee cited evidence of adverse outcomes with multifocal lenses, in contrast to toric lenses.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People undergoing cataract surgery whose eyes have an axial length less than 22.00 mm and no history of corneal refractive surgery.
decision_rules: The guideline bases its biometry formula recommendations on axial length.
The evidence reviewed for the original guideline found that Haigis and Hoffer Q had similar predictive accuracy in short eyes, whereas SRK/T performed poorly in this group.
The surveillance review does not propose changing the biometry formula recommendations.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The report describes the evidence underlying the existing recommendations but does not reproduce their instructions for this axial-length group.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People undergoing cataract surgery whose eyes have average or medium long axial lengths and no history of corneal refractive surgery.
decision_rules: The original evidence review identified Barrett Universal II and SRK/T as the best-performing formula options for average or medium long eyes.
The surveillance review does not propose changing the axial-length-based formula recommendations.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: These formula comparisons are findings from the original evidence base; the report does not reproduce the wording of the applicable guideline recommendations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People undergoing cataract surgery whose eyes have an axial length greater than 26.00 mm and no history of corneal refractive surgery.
decision_rules: The original evidence review found poor predictive performance with Hoffer Q in eyes with an axial length greater than 26.00 mm.
SRK/T did not show the same poor performance in very long eyes that it showed in short eyes.
The surveillance review does not propose changing the existing biometry formula recommendations.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The report does not state a preferred formula specifically for eyes with an axial length greater than 26.00 mm. The finding of poor Hoffer Q performance is not presented as an explicit recommendation against its use.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People undergoing cataract surgery who have previously had corneal refractive surgery.
decision_rules: The original evidence review could not identify a consistently superior biometry formula for this population because the findings were uncertain and heterogeneous.
The surveillance review does not propose changing the biometry formula recommendations.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The report discusses newer formula studies but does not adopt a study author's formula preference as a new guideline recommendation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People undergoing cataract surgery who require an intraocular lens.
decision_rules: NICE proposes an update concerning intraocular lens material and edge design to address prevention of posterior capsule opacification.

The original evidence suggested lower posterior capsule opacification rates with hydrophobic acrylic or silicone lenses than with hydrophilic acrylic or polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) lenses, and with square-edged rather than round-edged lenses.
The newer evidence continues to favour hydrophobic lenses and suggests that sharp-edged lenses are likely associated with less posterior capsule opacification than round-edged lenses.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Recommendations about lens material and design were removed during consultation on the original guideline. This report proposes developing or updating recommendations; it does not yet recommend a specific material or design.

decision_rules: The committee considered routine laser-assisted cataract surgery inappropriate and stated that its use could be justified only in clinical trials.
The surveillance review proposes no change to the surgical timing and technique recommendation.

not_recommended.name: laser-assisted cataract surgery
not_recommended.reason: The committee considered regular use inappropriate in light of the evidence, with use justified only within clinical trials. Subsequent evidence found little or no difference from standard PCS in the assessed complications, postoperative visual acuity and quality of life.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The report compares FLACS with standard PCS but does not reproduce an explicit current recommendation naming PCS as the preferred procedure.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People needing cataract surgery in both eyes who are at low risk of ocular complications during or after surgery.
decision_rules: The existing guideline offers simultaneous bilateral surgery as an option for patients at low risk of intraoperative or postoperative complications.
An immediate-versus-delayed surgery choice was considered for an update, but mixed expert and stakeholder feedback led to retention of the existing recommendations.

recommended_regimens.name: bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: An option under the existing guideline for people at low risk of complications during or after surgery.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence involved carefully selected, lower-risk patients. Studies were not large enough to establish whether approaches differ in rare but serious bilateral complications; the new review graded certainty from moderate to very low.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People needing cataract surgery in both eyes who require general anaesthesia when anaesthesia might carry risks.
decision_rules: The report describes the existing guideline as allowing simultaneous bilateral surgery for people requiring general anaesthesia when anaesthesia might carry risks.
A proposed clarification of the surgery choice was not adopted because expert and stakeholder views on its clinical appropriateness and safety did not reach a clear consensus.

recommended_regimens.name: bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: An option described in the retained recommendations for people requiring general anaesthesia when anaesthesia might carry risks.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The report does not establish the safety of simultaneous surgery in higher-risk patients. The wording offered for consultation was a proposed change, not an adopted recommendation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with preoperative astigmatism undergoing cataract surgery.
decision_rules: The committee did not explicitly advise against toric lenses; it instead made a positive recommendation about other strategies and a recommendation for research on toric-lens cost-effectiveness.
The newly submitted studies did not assess cost-effectiveness, so the surveillance review proposes no change to this area.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The report does not specify which alternative strategy the existing positive recommendation selects. Its research recommendation compares toric lenses with on-axis or limbal-relaxing incision surgery, or non-toric lenses without further intervention; those research comparators are not presented here as recommended regimens. The committee considered the demonstrated UCVA benefit insufficient to justify increased resource use without a clear quality-of-life advantage, but did not issue a recommendation against toric lenses.

therapies_index.name: cataract surgery
key_toxicities: Posterior capsule opacification can occur after surgery.

therapies_index.name: laser-assisted phacoemulsification cataract surgery
therapies_index.administration: The guideline committee considered its use justifiable only within clinical trials.

therapies_index.name: immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery (ISBCS)
approved_indications: The existing guideline recommendations cover people at low risk of complications during or after surgery and people requiring general anaesthesia for whom anaesthesia might carry risks.
therapies_index.administration: Both eyes are operated on during the same surgical episode.
key_toxicities: Rare, potentially catastrophic complications were a concern, but the cited studies were not sufficiently powered to detect bilateral endophthalmitis or bilateral blindness.

therapies_index.name: delayed sequential bilateral cataract surgery (DSBCS)
therapies_index.administration: The eyes are operated on at separate times.

therapies_index.name: intraocular lens (IOL) implantation
therapies_index.administration: An IOL is implanted during cataract surgery.

therapies_index.name: combined posterior chamber phakic intraocular lens (PC-pIOL) removal and cataract surgery
therapies_index.administration: PC-pIOL removal is performed together with cataract surgery.

therapies_index.name: Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy
approved_indications: Posterior capsule opacification after cataract surgery

therapies_index.name: toric lenses
approved_indications: Astigmatism in people undergoing cataract surgery
therapies_index.administration: Implantation may require additional preoperative assessment and surgical time; the committee did not explicitly recommend against these lenses.
key_toxicities: The guideline committee raised a concern that the added procedural complexity could increase intraoperative complications; it did not identify the adverse-outcome concerns it had seen with multifocal lenses.
monitoring: The committee discussed additional follow-up appointments to assess refractive correction.

therapies_index.name: accommodating intraocular lenses
therapies_index.administration: Implantation for cataract is addressed in related NICE interventional procedures guidance.

therapies_index.name: multifocal (nonaccommodative) intraocular lenses
therapies_index.administration: Implantation during cataract surgery is addressed in related NICE interventional procedures guidance.

therapies_index.name: non-diffractive extended depth of focus lenses
refractive design older version of multifocal IOLs
hydrophobic acrylic IOLs
key_toxicities: In the long-term follow-up reported by Yu et al. 2022, these IOLs had higher posterior capsule opacification values and Nd:YAG capsulotomy rates than silicone IOLs.

therapies_index.name: hydrophilic acrylic IOLs
key_toxicities: Cited evidence associated these IOLs with more posterior capsule opacification and Nd:YAG capsulotomy than hydrophobic acrylic IOLs.

therapies_index.name: polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) lenses
key_toxicities: The original guideline evidence indicated more posterior capsule opacification than with hydrophobic acrylic or silicone lenses.

therapies_index.name: round-edged IOLs
key_toxicities: The cited comparisons found more posterior capsule opacification than with square-edged or sharp-edged IOLs.

therapies_index.name: Vivinex XY1 IOL
therapies_index.administration: In Leydolt et al. 2024, participants received this IOL in one eye.
key_toxicities: Leydolt et al. 2024 assessed posterior capsule opacification and Nd:YAG capsulotomy after implantation.

therapies_index.name: Clareon CNA0T0 IOL
therapies_index.administration: In Leydolt et al. 2024, participants received this IOL in the other eye.
key_toxicities: Leydolt et al. 2024 assessed posterior capsule opacification and Nd:YAG capsulotomy after implantation.

therapies_index.name: AcrySof
therapies_index.administration: Implanted in the cataract surgery cohort examined by Ursell et al. 2018.
key_toxicities: Ursell et al. 2018 assessed posterior capsule opacification and Nd:YAG capsulotomy after implantation.

therapies_index.name: Rayone EMV RAO200E
therapies_index.administration: Implanted in eyes examined by McNeely et al. 2024.

therapies_index.name: Artis Symbiose IOLs
therapies_index.administration: Implanted in eyes examined by McNeely et al. 2024.

special_populations.considerations: Cataract prevalence increases with age: 24% at 70 to 74 years, 42% at 75 to 79 years, 59% at 80 to 84 years, and 71% in people over 85 years.

Donachie et al. 2023 reported slightly higher PCO rates in women than in men. The report notes that hormonal factors and the greater prevalence of conditions such as diabetes and uveitis in women may contribute to this difference.

special_populations.population: People at low risk of ocular complications during or after cataract surgery
special_populations.considerations: Studies of bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery selected people at low risk of complications. They were too small to establish differences in rare, severe complications.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The existing guideline presents bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery as an option for this population.

special_populations.population: People requiring general anaesthesia for cataract surgery when anaesthesia might carry risks
special_populations.considerations: The report identifies this group as eligible under the existing recommendations for consideration of bilateral simultaneous surgery.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The existing guideline presents bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery as an option for this population.

special_populations.population: People at higher risk of ocular complications, including those with ocular comorbidities
special_populations.considerations: The studies of bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery did not provide evidence about outcomes in this population. The report retains the existing recommendations rather than extending the option on the basis of the new evidence.

special_populations.population: People with a history of corneal refractive surgery
special_populations.considerations: In the evidence used to develop the guideline, no biometry formula produced consistently better results than the others for this population because the evidence was uncertain and heterogeneous.

Evidence reviewed for the guideline found improvements in uncorrected visual acuity, residual astigmatism and spectacle use with toric rather than non-toric lenses, but did not establish an effect on overall quality of life. The committee considered toric lenses unlikely to be cost-effective compared with standard monofocal lenses and did not explicitly recommend against them.

document_sections.heading: Surveillance proposal
document_sections.content: NICE proposes updating its adult cataract management guideline on intraocular lens selection. New evidence and professional input appear sufficient to revisit lens design and material in recommendations 1.4.1 and 1.4.4. They do not appear sufficient to revise recommendations on biometry formulas, surgical timing and technique, bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery, or toric lenses.

document_sections.heading: Context
document_sections.content: A UK audit by the Royal College of Ophthalmologists (RCOphth) prompted a review of intraocular lens selection. During that review, RCOphth supplied further evidence and feedback on lens selection and 4 other areas: biometry formulas (recommendations 1.3.5 to 1.3.8), surgical timing and technique (recommendation 1.6.1), bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery (recommendations 1.6.2 to 1.6.4), and toric lenses (recommendation for research 1).

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: NICE assessed the RCOphth UK audit, searched for systematic reviews and randomised controlled trials (RCTs) concerning intraocular lens (IOL) design and material for prevention of posterior capsule opacification (PCO), examined RCOphth submissions and the existing evidence across the 5 topics, and checked related NICE guidance, quality standards, and tracked events. It compared new information with current recommendations, sought expert views on bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery, and consulted stakeholders on that topic. Further details of surveillance procedures and possible decisions are available in the NICE guideline development manual.

document_sections.heading: Search and selection strategy
document_sections.content: The search sought new RCTs and systematic reviews comparing lens designs and materials for preventing PCO after cataract surgery. Systematic reviews were eligible from the previous search date, January 2017; RCTs were eligible from the systematic-review cut-off dates, January 2020. NICE did not search the other topics further because the submitted evidence was considered adequate for surveillance.

document_sections.heading: Related NICE guidance
document_sections.content: The search identified NICE's quality standard on serious eye disorders and interventional procedures guidance on accommodating intraocular lens implantation for cataract and on implantation of multifocal (nonaccommodative) intraocular lenses during cataract surgery.

document_sections.heading: Other related guidance
document_sections.content: Relevant UK documents were High flow cataract surgery (RCOphth and GRIFT, February 2022), Quality Standards for cataract services (RCOphth, December 2021), and Correct IOL implantation in cataract surgery (RCOphth, December 2021).

document_sections.heading: Evidence and intelligence considered in this review
document_sections.content: The report brings together original guideline evidence, relevant earlier surveillance findings, and new information for biometry formulas (recommendations 1.3.5 to 1.3.8), IOL selection (recommendations 1.4.1 and 1.4.4), toric lenses (recommendation for research 1), surgical timing and technique (recommendation 1.6.1), and bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery (recommendations 1.6.2 to 1.6.4).

document_sections.heading: Biometry formulas
document_sections.content: This topic concerns how formulas are selected for calculating IOL power.

document_sections.heading: Evidence considered when developing the guideline
document_sections.content: Recommendations 1.3.5 to 1.3.8 arose from a review of formulas for IOL biometry. It included 18 observational comparisons in previously unoperated eyes of varying axial lengths undergoing phacoemulsification and Six observational studies in eyes with previous corneal refractive surgery; it found no RCTs or economic evidence. The committee noted substantial statistical imprecision across formulas and outcomes. In eyes without previous corneal refractive surgery, SRK/T performed poorly at axial lengths less than 22.00 mm, unlike at lengths greater than 26.00 mm; Hoffer Q performed poorly above 26.00 mm. Haigis ranked among the best choices for 3 of the 4 axial-length subgroups. At short lengths, Hoffer Q and Haigis had similar predictive accuracy; Barrett Universal II and SRK/T performed best at average or medium long lengths. Among eyes with prior corneal refractive surgery, uncertainty and heterogeneity prevented identification of a consistently superior formula.

document_sections.heading: New evidence
document_sections.content: Of 11 submitted studies, 4 were ineligible and 7 were included. In a retrospective chart review, Blehm et al. 2024 examined 445 eyes of 247 patients measured preoperatively with Argos. Barrett Universal II (BUII) was used for IOL calculations and BTAL for retrospective calculations; outcomes included absolute prediction error (APE), refraction, monocular uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA), and corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA). Mean APE was 0.36 ± 0.33 diopters (D) with BUII and 0.34 ± 0.32 D with BTAL. BTAL had significantly lower APE and a higher percentage of eyes with APE of 0.5 D or less among short eyes; differences were not significant for medium or long eyes. The authors considered both formulas highly accurate, with a possible BTAL advantage in short eyes. Cione et al. August 2024 retrospectively compared 554 operated long eyes in groups of 26.00≤AL<28.00 mm, 28.00≤AL<30.00 mm, and AL≥30.00 mm. They assessed 8 formulas not requiring ACD—BUII, Emmetropia Verifying Optical (EVO) 2.0, Ladas Super Formula (LSF), Hoffer Q, Holladay 1, SRKT, T2, and T2.2—using constants from ULIB and IOLCon. Measures included mean absolute error (MAE), median absolute error (MedAE), and proportions within ±0.50 and ±1.00 diopters (D) of prediction. T2-ALu performed best from 26.00 mm to 28.00 mm, EVO 2.0-ALc from 28.00 mm to 30.00 mm, and EVO 2.0-CMALe at AL≥30.00 mm; the authors favoured matching formula and AL adjustment to the subrange. Cione et al. September 2024 retrospectively studied 150 eyes of 160 patients with previous myopic Photorefractive Keratectomy (PRK) or laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) after uncomplicated cataract surgery and IOL implantation. They assessed ALMA prediction error (PE), SRKT nominal and optimised A-Constants from ULIB and IOL Con, and decreased ULIB optimised constant (DUOC) factors of -1.2 to -1.5. Outcomes were MedAE and proportions within ±0.50 and ±1.00 diopters (D). ALMA with ULIB nominal constants yielded lower MedAE and more eyes within 1.0 D; DUOC (-1.3) significantly improved MedAE and the proportion within ±0.50 D. The authors recommended ALMA with DUOC of -1.3 when optimised constants are unavailable and called for further study of constants after laser refractive surgery (LRS). Kojima et al. 2024 retrospectively assessed 461 eyes of 461 patients, with mean age 73.8 ± 8.4 years, comparing predicted refractive error (PRE) from SRI (ARGOS) and equivalent refractive index (ERI) biometers (IOLMaster 700). Constants were derived in a learning group and tested in a validation group. With SRK/T and BUII (BU II), optimised SRI constants produced significantly smaller validation-group PRE than the ERI biometer. Optimisation significantly improved arithmetic PRE for Barrett UII with SRI in long (group L) and short (group S) eyes. The authors concluded that SRI constant optimisation improved postoperative refraction. McNeely et al. 2024 evaluated SRK/T, HofferQ, Holladay 1, Haigis, MM, BUII, EVO, and AS-OCT ray tracing in 100 eyes receiving Rayone EMV RAO200E or Artis Symbiose IOLs, using IOLMaster 700 and MS-39 AS-OCT measurements. Outcomes were MAE, MedAE, and proportions within ±0.25, ±0.50, ±0.75, and ±1.00 diopters (D). For enhanced monofocal IOLs, MM yielded the highest proportion within ±0.75 D (96%) and EVO the lowest MAE and MedAE; for multifocal IOLs, SRK/T yielded the highest proportion within ±0.75 D (94%), and ray tracing the lowest MAE and MedAE. The authors reported high accuracy overall and accuracy for MM and ray tracing comparable with established formulas. Shammas et al. 2024 retrospectively analysed 2 series after myopic laser vision correction (M-LVC): a BPEI training series of 330 eyes for a revised Shammas-Cooke corneal-power equation and a DMEI testing series of 165 eyes comparing it with Shammas PL, Haigis-L, and Barrett True-K NH on the ASCRS calculator. Mean PE was 0.09 ± 0.56 diopters (D) for Shammas-Cooke, -0.44 ± 0.61 D for Shammas PL, -0.47 ± 0.59 D for Haigis-L, and -0.18 ± 0.56 D for Barrett True-K NH; corresponding MAE values were 0.43 D, 0.60 D, 0.61 D, and 0.45 D. The respective proportions within ±0.50 D were 66.7%, 47.9%, 48.5%, and 65.5%. The authors found Shammas-Cooke better than Shammas PL and Haigis-L and similar to Barrett True-K NH. Zeng et al. 2024 retrospectively studied 24 eyes of 24 patients having posterior chamber phakic intraocular lens (PC-pIOL) removal alongside cataract surgery in China. IOLMaster 700 measured AL and anterior-segment parameters. They assessed SRK/T, Holladay 1, and Haigis with or without Wang-Koch (WK) AL adjustment, plus Barrett Universal II [BUII], Emmetropia Verifying Optical [EVO] v2.0, Kane, and Pearl-DGS. MedAE ranged from 0.33 with EVO 2.0 to 1.32 with Holladay 1; root-mean-square absolute error (RMS AE) ranged from 0.591 with Haigis-WKC1 to 1.513 with Holladay 1. Errors in ACD and lens thickness (LT) measurement had negligible effects for BUII and EVO 2.0. The authors reported strong prediction accuracy for Kane, EVO 2.0, and traditional formulas with WK adjustment, without a significant effect of ACD or LT measurement errors in highly myopic PC-pIOL eyes.

document_sections.heading: System intelligence
document_sections.content: RCOphth reported wider use of the Barrett IOL formula since 2017.

document_sections.heading: Comparison of new evidence and intelligence with the guideline evidence base
document_sections.content: Earlier evidence favoured Haigis in 3 of the 4 AL subgroups, found Hoffer Q similarly accurate to Haigis in short eyes, and favoured BUII and SRK/T at average or medium long lengths. It did not establish a consistently superior formula after corneal refractive surgery, so existing recommendations vary by axial length. New studies spanned formulas, IOLs, measurement platforms, axial lengths, and patient groups. No formula appeared best across lengths; several performed accurately, some findings called for further research, and heterogeneous Barrett evidence generally supported existing recommendations. NICE judged the evidence insufficient to revise biometry-formula recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Intraocular lenses selection
document_sections.content: This topic addresses whether lens material and optic design affect PCO and postoperative vision.

document_sections.heading: Evidence considered when developing the guideline
document_sections.content: The reviews underpinning recommendations 1.4.1 and 1.4.4 examined square-edged versus round-edge and plate versus loop designs, and hydrophilic acrylic, hydrophobic acrylic, collagen, hydroxyethyl methacrylate-based, and silicone-based materials for PCO prevention. This was combined with a question on aspheric versus spheric and plate versus loop designs for refractive outcomes and optical aberrations. A Cochrane review of 31 RCTs by Findl et al. 2010 and 44 further RCTs yielded 75 RCTs: 27 compared materials, 23 compared aspheric with spheric lenses, 18 compared 1-piece (loop or plate) with 3-piece lenses, and 15 compared square-edged with round-edged lenses. Evidence suggested less PCO with hydrophobic acrylic or silicone than with hydrophilic acrylic or polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), and with square-edged than round-edged IOLs. Consultation uncertainty led to removal of material and design recommendations pending further consideration.

document_sections.heading: New evidence
document_sections.content: The rapid search identified 4 systematic reviews, 2 RCTs, and 1 UK cohort study. RCOphth submitted another 10 studies; 9 were already found or ineligible, while the additional UK real-world study by Ursell et al. 2018 was included.

document_sections.heading: Systematic reviews
document_sections.content: Maedel et al. 2021 reviewed 10 studies involving 1,065 participants and judged sharp-edged IOLs likely to produce less PCO and fewer neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) capsulotomies than round-edged IOLs. Clearer vision was possible, but the visual-acuity effect was less certain; the authors sought standardised PCO assessment and research on quality of life and adverse events. Wu et al. 2020 analysed 13 RCTs with 939 patients and found significantly lower PCO scores and fewer Nd:YAG capsulotomies with hydrophobic than hydrophilic acrylic IOLs. The authors considered hydrophobic acrylic lenses more effective after cataract surgery, particularly in Western countries. Yu et al. 2022 reviewed 17 studies and found higher PCO values and Nd:YAG capsulotomy rates with hydrophobic acrylic than silicone IOLs at long-term follow-up (≥6 years). The authors considered long-term complications more substantial with hydrophobic acrylic lenses despite their use to reduce complications and optimise vision. Zhao et al. 2017 included 11 studies with 889 eyes/patients and found lower Nd:YAG capsulotomy rates and subjective and estimated PCO scores with hydrophobic than hydrophilic IOLs, without a significant visual-acuity difference. The authors judged hydrophobic lenses better at reducing PCO and capsulotomy.

document_sections.heading: RCTs
document_sections.content: Leydolt et al. 2024 compared 2 hydrophobic acrylic IOLs over 3 years in an RCT of 100 patients, with Vivinex XY1 in one eye and Clareon CNA0T0 in the other; 67 patients were assessed after 3 years. PCO scores were 1.0 ± 1.0 with Vivinex XY1 and 1.5 ± 1.2 with Clareon CNA0T0, a statistically significant difference. Nd:YAG capsulotomy rates were 7.5% and 9.0%, respectively, without a significant difference. Both lenses had low PCO and capsulotomy rates, with a small advantage for Vivinex XY1. Sheetal et al. 2023 compared Optiflex Genesis, Eyecryl Plus (ASHFY 600), and Tecnis-1 in an RCT involving 159 eyes from 140 patients. At 1 year, visual acuity, refractive accuracy, higher-order aberrations, contrast sensitivity, and PCO did not differ significantly. Safety, efficacy, and satisfaction were similar, with no major complications reported; longer follow-up was needed.

document_sections.heading: UK real-world evidence
document_sections.content: Donachie et al. 2023 studied 500,872 cataract operations in the Royal College of Ophthalmologists' National Ophthalmology Database. PCO affected 12.3% of eyes and became more frequent over time. Identified risk factors were hydrophilic IOL material, AL >26 mm, high myopia, lower IOL power, prior vitrectomy, younger age, and female gender. The authors identified IOL material as a potentially modifiable factor. Ursell et al. 2018 retrospectively examined patients aged 65 and older who received acrylic monofocal IOLs between 2010 and 2013 at 7 UK clinics. Among AcrySof, other hydrophobic, and hydrophilic acrylic cohorts, AcrySof had significantly lower 3-year PCO and Nd:YAG capsulotomy incidence. Non-AcrySof cohorts had higher capsulotomy odds ratios (OR), including in a single-piece IOL subgroup. The authors considered AcrySof superior for these outcomes within 3 years after implantation.

document_sections.heading: System intelligence
document_sections.content: An RCOphth 2021 feasibility report used National Ophthalmology Database (NOD) Cataract Audit information from 601,084 operations by 2,566 surgeons in 58 centres. Recorded PCO rates were 4% at 1 year, 18.0% at 3 years, and 31% at 5 years. Rates were higher for many models and centres and for lenses containing a hydrophilic component; hydrophobic and silicone IOLs had lower rates than hydrophilic lenses. Differences in how centres recorded PCO over time complicated comparisons between models. Patients could not be linked across centres when cataract surgery and PCO YAG occurred at different sites. The report's authors urged better PCO recording and comparison across IOLs. They also argued that the £132 cost of YAG laser capsulotomy would probably outweigh IOL price differences, making cheaper lenses with higher PCO rates a likely false economy for the NHS. RCOphth additionally anticipated clinical support for revising these recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Comparison of new evidence and intelligence with the guideline evidence base
document_sections.content: Earlier evidence indicated that hydrophobic acrylic or silicone and square-edged IOLs might reduce PCO, but consultation challenges led to withdrawal of design and material recommendations. New findings continue to favour hydrophobic materials and suggest sharp edges are likely associated with less PCO than round edges. NICE considers the combined evidence sufficient to develop recommendations on material and design for PCO reduction; RCOphth input suggests practice would probably support an update.

document_sections.heading: Surgical timing and technique
document_sections.content: This topic compares laser-assisted cataract surgery with standard phacoemulsification and considers whether existing guidance should change.

document_sections.heading: Evidence considered when developing the guideline
document_sections.content: Recommendation 1.6.1 was based on a comparison of laser-assisted with standard ultrasound phacoemulsification. Across 16 studies, no clinical difference was suggested. The only statistically significant finding was a 1 to 1.5 letter gain in corrected visual acuity at 6 months; the committee judged it clinically unimportant because it did not recur at other assessments and uncorrected visual acuity did not differ. In 1 economic study using simulated complication rates and an assumed 5% visual-acuity improvement in uncomplicated cases, laser-assisted surgery yielded 0.06 quality adjusted life years (QALYs) but cost more; its incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) was $AUS92,862 per QALY gained, above conventional cost-effectiveness thresholds. The committee considered routine laser-assisted surgery inappropriate and its use justifiable only in clinical trials. It did not consider a recommendation for further trials necessary, particularly because trials were under way. FEMCAT and FACT were subsequently monitored through the NICE tracker.

document_sections.heading: Evidence considered in the 2021 exceptional surveillance review focused on surgical timing
document_sections.content: Publication of the FEMCAT trial (Schweitzer et al. 2020) and FACT trial (Day et al. 2021) prompted the 2021 review. Those RCTs found no clinically meaningful differences between femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS) and PCS in visual acuity or intraoperative and postoperative complications; at its then-current cost, FLACS was not considered cost-effective. Findings on astigmatism among patients with substantial preoperative astigmatism were mixed, so the trial authors saw a possible reason for continued FLACS-versus-phacoemulsification (PCS) research in that subgroup. Surveillance reviewers considered further meta-analysis necessary to estimate rare-event effects more precisely and improve the generalisability of individual studies. The Cochrane Eyes and Vision group reported that an update of its 2016 comparison was under way. NICE proposed no guideline update at that time.

document_sections.heading: New evidence
document_sections.content: Of 14 studies submitted concerning recommendation 1.6.1, all had either been considered in the 2021 surveillance review or were unsuitable under the evidence-review criteria. The subsequently published Narayan et al. 2023 Cochrane review included 42 RCTs comparing FLACS with standard PCS. It found little or no difference in intraoperative or postoperative complications, postoperative visual acuity, or quality of life. Its authors called for more safety and efficacy research using standardised outcomes.

document_sections.heading: System intelligence
document_sections.content: RCOphth noted that femtosecond-laser cataract-surgery evidence was now available and suggested its outcomes were similar to those of conventional cataract surgery.

document_sections.heading: Comparison of new evidence and intelligence with the guideline evidence base
document_sections.content: Earlier evidence found no clinical difference between FLACS and PCS and suggested that FLACS was unlikely to be cost-effective. The newer Cochrane review likewise found little or no difference and called for further research. NICE found no reason to change this part of the guideline.

document_sections.heading: Bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery
document_sections.content: This topic compares surgery on both eyes in immediate sequence with operations separated in time.

document_sections.heading: Evidence considered when developing the guideline
document_sections.content: Recommendations 1.6.2 to 1.6.4 drew on a comparison of bilateral simultaneous, or rapid sequential, surgery with unilateral eye surgery. The 3 included RCTs found no meaningful difference in intraoperative, postoperative, or serious postoperative complications between simultaneous and sequential groups. In 1 published economic study, immediate sequential surgery was more effective and cheaper than delayed sequential surgery, although uncertainty around cost-effectiveness could not be estimated reliably. The committee considered the recruited groups' long-term visual outcomes similar, but identified 2 major evidence limits: samples were too small to detect differences in rare catastrophic events, and trials selected only patients at low risk of operative or postoperative complications. Outcomes in higher-risk patients, including those with ocular comorbidities, therefore remained unknown. The committee consequently considered simultaneous surgery an option only for the low-risk population represented in the trials.

document_sections.heading: New evidence
document_sections.content: Of 6 submitted studies, 2 were already in the guideline evidence base and 3 were ineligible under the review protocol. Dickman et al. 2022, the remaining Cochrane review, included 14 studies, including 2 RCTs already in the guideline, and 276,260 participants. It compared immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery (ISBCS) with delayed sequential bilateral cataract surgery (DSBCS). Refractive outcomes did not differ significantly at 1 to 3 months, and intraoperative and postoperative complications showed no major difference, although study heterogeneity was significant. Evidence about comparative endophthalmitis risk was limited: unilateral endophthalmitis was very rare in both groups and bilateral endophthalmitis was not reported. None of the studies had sufficient power to detect bilateral endophthalmitis, and all enrolled low-risk patients. Economic estimates were unreliable because of flawed assumptions, although every study reported lower costs with ISBCS. The review authors judged clinically important outcome differences between immediate and delayed surgery unlikely and costs lower with immediate surgery, while stressing limited evidence, certainty graded moderate to very low, and a need for well-designed cost-effectiveness studies.

document_sections.heading: System intelligence
document_sections.content: RCOphth reported that the annual proportion of ISBCS has fallen since a modest increase during COVID. It suggested NICE guidance might partly contribute to low use and that conducting most cataract operations on 2 separate occasions could waste resources.

document_sections.heading: Topic experts
document_sections.content: NICE sought views on a possible small change to recommendation 1.6.3 that would offer a choice between immediate sequential bilateral surgery and first-eye surgery followed by delayed second-eye surgery for people at low risk of ocular complications during or after surgery or those needing general anaesthesia when it carries increased complication risk. Experts were also asked whether the procedure's name is usual NHS terminology and whether patients or carers might understand 'immediate' as an urgent appointment. Of 10 experts contacted, including RCOphth, 6 responded: 4 supported the proposed clinical change and 2 did not. Concerns included implementation in teaching hospitals or complex case mixes, possible total blindness, and patient acceptability. One expert reported little or no use of general anaesthesia and questioned its importance; another considered anaesthesia generally risky because most cataract patients are older and saw no need to specify increased risk of complications or distress. All 6 considered the terminology usual in practice, although 1 questioned its grammar and suggested alternative wording.

document_sections.heading: Consultation
document_sections.content: Because expert opinion lacked consensus, NICE consulted on the proposed minor revision. Of 7 stakeholders who commented, 2 disagreed, and consensus was again absent.

document_sections.heading: Comparison of new evidence and intelligence with the guideline evidence base
document_sections.content: Original trials found no major long-term visual-outcome difference between same-day and different-day surgery in their selected populations. They were too small to resolve rare catastrophic complications, including blindness, and did not provide evidence for patients at higher risk, such as those with ocular comorbidities. Existing recommendations therefore restrict simultaneous surgery to low-risk patients or those needing general anaesthesia when anaesthesia may pose risks. The Cochrane review reached similar comparative findings, but 2 of its trials were already in the guideline and its other studies were observational. None could adequately detect rare serious outcomes such as bilateral blindness, and all studied lower-risk patients. Although NICE initially proposed a minor recommendation change, mixed expert and stakeholder responses left its clinical appropriateness and safety without clear consensus. NICE decided to retain the existing recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Toric lenses for astigmatism
document_sections.content: This topic addresses outcomes and cost-effectiveness of toric lenses for patients with astigmatism.

document_sections.heading: Evidence considered when developing the guideline
document_sections.content: Recommendation for research 1 asks about NHS cost-effectiveness of toric lenses versus on-axis or limbal-relaxing incision surgery, or non-toric lenses without further intervention, across the entire preoperative-to-postoperative care pathway and by preoperative astigmatism level. The preceding review of on-axis surgery and limbal-relaxing incisions identified 1 systematic review of 8 RCTs and 4 additional RCTs. Compared with non-toric lenses, toric lenses improved uncorrected visual acuity, reduced residual astigmatism, and reduced spectacle use, but evidence did not establish an effect on overall quality of life. One American economic study suggested possible lifetime savings in patient spending on spectacles or contact lenses; it had serious limitations. The committee thought toric lenses' acquisition price was unlikely to substantially exceed standard monofocal prices, but anticipated a substantial NHS resource burden: potentially an extra preoperative visit, corneal-topography biometry unavailable at some centres, additional operating time estimated at 5 plus extra minutes, and equipment such as toric markers. It also raised possible extra visits to assess refractive correction, poor visual satisfaction if patients could not obtain toric lenses in both eyes, procedural complexity, possible intraoperative complications, and staff-training needs. Those factors were absent from the presented cost-utility analysis. The committee considered the observed relative UCVA benefit, without corresponding evidence of relative BCVA improvement, insufficient to justify extra resources. It expected very small QALY gains from spectacle independence and noted that many patients would still need reading glasses. Without a demonstrated quality-of-life advantage over standard monofocal lenses, it considered toric lenses unlikely to be cost-effective for astigmatism. Unlike multifocal lenses, toric lenses had not raised evidence-based adverse-outcome concerns. The committee therefore did not explicitly recommend against them; it made a positive recommendation about alternative approaches and set a research recommendation.

document_sections.heading: New evidence
document_sections.content: The enquirer supplied 11 studies, none of which assessed cost-effectiveness, the committee's principal unresolved concern.

document_sections.heading: System intelligence
document_sections.content: RCOphth described a shift towards enhanced monofocal IOLs in the NHS during the past 2 years. It stated that evidence favoured newer non-diffractive extended depth of focus lenses for distance and intermediate vision and that diffractive design trifocal IOLs provided better near vision with less glare and fewer halos than older refractive design multifocal IOLs.

document_sections.heading: Comparison of new evidence and intelligence with the guideline evidence base
document_sections.content: Earlier studies favoured toric over non-toric lenses for uncorrected visual acuity, residual astigmatism, and spectacle use, but did not establish a quality-of-life effect. Cost-effectiveness concerns led to recommendation for research 1. Because the newly submitted studies did not include cost-effectiveness analyses, NICE found no impact on the guideline.

document_sections.heading: Budget impact
document_sections.content: If different IOL designs or materials lowered PCO incidence, fewer YAG laser treatments could release resources. RCOphth cited NHS Digital figures of over 60,000 YAG capsulotomy HRGs in England in 2018/19, at a mean £132 each, equivalent to approximately £8 million a year.

document_sections.heading: System impact
document_sections.content: Lowering PCO through IOL design or material could reduce YAG procedures and release staff time.

document_sections.heading: Population impact
document_sections.content: Cataracts are usually age-related, and prevalence rises with age: 24% at 70 to 74 years, 42% at 75 to 79 years, 59% at 80 to 84 years, and 71% over 85 years, according to CKS Cataracts. Cataract surgery is the UK's most common operation, with around 472,000 procedures each year in the NHS in England and Wales. RCOphth 2021 describes PCO as a frequent postoperative complication, affecting roughly 1 in 5 operated eyes.

document_sections.heading: Environmental sustainability
document_sections.content: Preventing PCO might reduce appointments and YAG laser use, potentially supporting environmental sustainability in line with Delivering a Net Zero NHS and other NHS guidance.

document_sections.heading: Health inequalities
document_sections.content: Guideline development identified no particular inequality concerning IOL design and PCO. Donachie et al. 2023 reported slightly more PCO among women than men. The report notes that hormonal factors and a greater prevalence among women of conditions such as diabetes and uveitis may influence that difference.

document_sections.heading: How this fits with NHS and NICE priorities
document_sections.content: The NICE forward view does not expressly mention ophthalmology, although NICE aims to provide usable content. Ophthalmology is described as the busiest secondary-care outpatient specialty and accounts for almost 10% of the waiting list (NHS England 2023). Reducing PCO would likely release capacity and shorten waiting lists.

document_sections.heading: Overall impact on the guideline
document_sections.content: Surveillance examined 5 areas: biometry formular (recommendations 1.3.5 to 1.3.8), intraocular lens selection (recommendations 1.4.1 and 1.4.4), toric lenses (recommendation for research 1), surgical timing and technique (recommendation 1.6.1), and bilateral simultaneous surgery (recommendations 1.6.2 to 1.6.4). Only evidence on IOL design and materials was judged likely to affect the guideline; it indicated lower PCO rates with hydrophobic and potentially silicone lenses.

document_sections.heading: Overall proposal
document_sections.content: NICE proposes updating its adult cataract management guideline specifically on IOL material and design within intraocular lens selection.
